content:
Moving keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro pad is the most effective productivity boost I've ever made.

My journey into keyboard shortcuts

My first foray into keyboard shortcuts started with simple macOS text replacements, like using @@ to enter my primary email address, and similarly setting up common information such as my full name, address, phone number, and postal code.

I then decided to take shortcuts to another level with Keyboard Maestro, setting up keyboard shortcuts to open frequently used folders and applications.

From Desktop to Downloads, and various work-related folders, it's become pure muscle memory—pressing Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 instantly takes me where I'd otherwise need several clicks to reach. Other function keys are dedicated to opening frequently used apps and websites, as well as launching Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

Later, I went further to automate parts of my workflow, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching Shure PlusMOTIV whenever a specific USB-C microphone is connected.

Soon I began customizing shortcuts for tools, settings, and panels in Adobe Audition, with some immediately reassigned to the Logitech MX Master's gesture button for even faster editing.

Stepping it up

I used this setup for a long time, until one day Gui Rambo from 9to5Mac told me about a small macro pad he'd bought with 12 keys and 3 knobs. I was immediately hooked and bought the same one.

Once the keypad arrived, I discovered there's a bit of extra setup to get it working properly on macOS. Luckily, this GitHub project did most of the heavy lifting, and ChatGPT helped me finish the rest.

The beauty of this setup is having a dedicated keypad to trigger Keyboard Maestro shortcuts—meaning no memorization required, and no worrying about ergonomics.

Plus, this keypad supports up to 3 layers of 12 keys each, and the knobs can also function as buttons. This means I can use one layout while working in Adobe Audition, and a completely different one for operating system tasks.

When working in Adobe Audition, combining the MX Master gesture button with this macro pad makes switching tools, exporting files (or exporting specific sections), and applying effects like volume normalization, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, and ripple delete faster and smoother than using regular keyboard shortcuts—or no shortcuts at all—by orders of magnitude.

For operating system tasks, I can use another layer on the same keypad to switch audio inputs, adjust volume, tweak screen brightness, toggle microphone mute, and quickly open frequently used folders.

Honestly, memorizing all these commands does take a little time, but it becomes second nature faster than you'd think. More importantly, once you're used to it, your Mac feels broken without it.

What's more, there are tons of different macro pad configurations and options on the market—shapes, sizes, keys, knobs, lighting colors—you name it. This rabbit hole goes deep. If your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend giving it a try.
